newsitem.title: USA: U.S. crude outlook - pressure to consolidate rallies.
newsitem.headline: U.S. crude outlook - pressure to consolidate rallies.

text.p: U.S. crude prices will remain in bullish price territory next week, but see heightened pressure to consolidate and pull back from recent highs as fundamentals become more balanced, industry analysts said.
Sources said heating oil losses on the NYMEX last week reflected feelings the market had become overbought, despite extremely low distillate inventories.
"Traders that made money will cash in," said Paulo Nery, senior consultant for The Pace Consultants Inc. in Houston.
Nery also noted low distillate stocks still leave the market wide open to a cold weather price rally.
Tom Bentz, energy analyst at ING Derivatives in New York, said crude and products prices will consolidate in the near-term, decline after that, and then head upwards again.
"We are still in a bullish market, and I would still buy the pullback," said Bentz, noting spot crude will "chop around" between $23.90 and $25.60 for the near-term.
Working hand-in-hand with the supply shifts, is the narrow spread between West Texas Intermediate and Brent values, leaving the arbitrage window firmly closed, traders said.

"North Sea margins are good, so the crude is being sucked up over there. West African crudes, priced off Brent have been made expensive to bring to the U.S. market with such a small discount to the WTI," noted Rita Beale, energy analyst for Fimat in Houston.
The lack of North Sea and West African barrels will continue to prop domestic crude prices, a trend seen last week especially for Lousiana sweet grades.
"Domestic crudes have gained from the fact it's the cheaper crude of choice. LLS (Light Lousiana Sweet) is preferred...there is no Brent, no competition," Beale said.
Besides the constant weather watch for cold snaps in the East Coast, and storm developments, the market keeps one eye firmly planted on Iraq and the United Nations.

Analysts said statements from the United Nations last week, saying the time was not ripe for implementing the oil-for-food accord, furthered theories there will not be any Iraqi oil entering markets soon.
